VOLCANOES.name: Kīlauea
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE LIVING SURFACE
VOLCANOES.headline: The ground is never finished.
VOLCANOES.lead: Follow a lava channel across the lower East Rift Zone and encounter a landscape altered in months.
VOLCANOES.description: On 3 May 2018, fissures opened along Kīlauea’s lower East Rift Zone. By the time the eruption ended in September, lava had covered approximately 35.5 square kilometres. At the summit, repeated collapse events reshaped Halemaʻumaʻu.
VOLCANOES.question: How does molten rock redraw a coastline?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: This interpretive route illustrates the sequence from a new vent to established channel and the coast. It is not a measured flow map.
VOLCANOES.note1desc: In an established channel, the cooling surface becomes darker while incandescent lava continues moving beneath and between fragments.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: The 2018 lava flows covered roads and neighbourhoods. These are geological observations, but also records of lives and infrastructure changed.

VOLCANOES.name: Reykjanes
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE FRACTURE
VOLCANOES.headline: Sometimes the mountain is a line.
VOLCANOES.lead: Watch the geography of a rift tell a different eruption story: not a single summit, but an opening in the ground.
VOLCANOES.description: Repeated fissure eruptions on the Reykjanes Peninsula since December 2023 have made the region a remarkable location for observing rifting, surface cracking and lava-field growth.
VOLCANOES.question: What happens when the surface opens?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: Alter the conceptual extent of a fissure to reveal how linear eruptions differ from a central crater. Distances are illustrative.
VOLCANOES.factLabel: start of the Sundhnúkur eruption sequence
VOLCANOES.note1desc: Reykjanes straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates diverge and magma can move along fissure systems.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: The landscape evolves through repeated episodes. One photograph cannot communicate the succession of new openings and flows.

VOLCANOES.name: Mount St. Helens
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE COLLAPSE
VOLCANOES.headline: The shape of what is missing.
VOLCANOES.lead: The event of May 18, 1980 did not simply cover the landscape. It removed a large part of a mountain.
VOLCANOES.description: The north flank collapsed during the 1980 eruption. The summit lost roughly 400 metres in height, and a horseshoe-shaped crater opened toward the north. Later eruptions built lava domes within it.
VOLCANOES.question: Can an absence become the evidence?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: Adjust a simplified missing-flank overlay to understand the change in the mountain’s outline. Not a geodetic reconstruction.
VOLCANOES.note1desc: Instead of only building a cone, this event reshaped its entire silhouette through landslide and lateral blast.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: USGS distributes pre-eruption and later elevation models that can support a properly aligned, quantitative terrain comparison.

VOLCANOES.name: Etna
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE ACCUMULATION
VOLCANOES.headline: One mountain. Many surfaces.
VOLCANOES.lead: Study a volcanic landscape assembled by successive flows, cones and fractures rather than by a single eruption.
VOLCANOES.description: Mount Etna has built its shape through countless episodes of lava effusion, explosive activity and flank eruptions. Different deposits tell different chapters of its history.
VOLCANOES.question: How does repeated eruption build terrain?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: Select a conceptual deposit layer. Colours and thicknesses explain relative accumulation, not a measured cross-section of Etna.
VOLCANOES.note1desc: New deposits can obscure older surfaces and change flow pathways. An eruption can both destroy and construct.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: Geological mapping can identify material, age and extent—even when only a fraction of the eruption is directly observed.

VOLCANOES.name: Tajogaite
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE AFTERMATH
VOLCANOES.headline: What remains after the glow fades?
VOLCANOES.lead: Track the geographical and human aftermath of the eruption on La Palma in 2021.
VOLCANOES.description: The 2021 eruption on La Palma created a new cone, extensive lava fields and changed sections of the coastline. Its aftermath continues through cooling, surveying and adaptation.
VOLCANOES.question: What does a new landscape cost?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: Scrub an illustrative sequence of terrain covered by a lava field. The changing shapes are a concept visual, not a satellite comparison.
VOLCANOES.note1desc: Lava entering the Atlantic built new coastal platforms where land and ocean meet.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: A scientific atlas should also recognise settlements, livelihoods and cultural landscapes transformed by eruptions.

VOLCANOES.name: Vesuvius
VOLCANOES.subtitle: THE BURIED WORLD
VOLCANOES.headline: The ground remembers for us.
VOLCANOES.lead: Investigate the layers left by the 79 CE eruption and how buried deposits preserve a partial record.
VOLCANOES.description: The 79 CE eruption buried Roman settlements under ash and pyroclastic material. Geological stratigraphy and archaeology together help reconstruct its sequence and effects.
VOLCANOES.question: What can buried layers tell us?
VOLCANOES.moduleText: Reveal a stylised stratigraphic sequence. Layer labels illustrate geological principles and are not a measured excavation section.
VOLCANOES.factLabel: date of the documented Pompeii eruption
VOLCANOES.note1desc: Tephra layers, buildings and surviving accounts contain different kinds of evidence—none of them tells the whole story alone.
VOLCANOES.note2desc: Any model of the ancient landscape is interpretive. Uncertainty should remain visible in the design.
